opus-5.5.text:
I think we're closer than most people expect, but it depends a lot on what you mean by "competent colleague." If you mean something that can take a well-scoped task, go off for a while, use tools, recover from its own mistakes, and come back with something genuinely useful, we're already seeing early versions of that, and I'd guess within the next year or two it becomes pretty normal for a lot of knowledge work.

The harder part is the stuff that makes a human colleague feel like a colleague rather than a tool. You don't have to re-explain everything every time. They remember what you care about, they learn how you like things done, and they know when to ask you a question and when to just make a call. A lot of that comes down to memory, long-horizon reliability, and judgment, not raw intelligence. The models are already smart enough for a surprising amount of this. What's missing is the system around them: how they keep context over weeks rather than minutes, how they learn from feedback, and how they handle ambiguity without either bothering you constantly or going off the rails.

So my honest answer is that for narrow domains it's basically here, and for something that feels like a broadly capable coworker you trust with real responsibility, I'd say a few years. Not decades. And I think the gap closes faster than people think once agents can learn continuously from working alongside you, because that's what really compounds.

r001.rationale: The candidate predicts that broadly capable AI coworkers people can trust will arrive “in a few years,” and says the gap will close faster than people think.

fable-5.1.text:
I think closer than most people assume, and further than the demos suggest, and both of those are true at the same time.

Here's the way I'd break it down. A competent colleague isn't someone who's brilliant in a single five-minute window. It's someone who can take a vaguely specified task, go away for a week, hit a bunch of problems you didn't anticipate, make reasonable calls on most of them, come back and ask you about the two or three that actually matter, and ship something you'd put your name on. The "brilliant in five minutes" part, we basically have. The models are already better than most engineers at a well-posed problem with a clear spec. What we don't fully have yet is the week.

The reason the week is hard isn't really raw intelligence. It's that the number of things that can go slightly wrong compounds. If an agent is 99% reliable on each small decision and a real task is a few thousand small decisions, the probability it finishes without going off the rails is not 99%, it's close to zero. So the whole game right now is driving that per-step error rate down, and crucially giving the model the ability to notice when it's drifted and correct, rather than confidently continuing down a wrong path. That's a different capability than being smart. Humans are actually not that smart at the single-step level, but we're very good at going "hm, wait, that's weird" and backing up.

What's changed in the last year or so is that we've gotten much better at training for that specifically. Long-horizon reinforcement learning, where the model is rewarded for actually completing the real task and not just producing plausible-looking text, turns out to be the thing. You put the model in an environment, you let it run for a long time, you let it make mistakes, and you train on whether the end state is right. When you do that, you see the reliability curve bend in a way you just don't get from scaling pretraining alone.

So my honest answer: for software engineering specifically, I think we're within a couple of years of agents that a strong team would genuinely treat as a colleague, meaning you give them tickets, not prompts. In some narrow domains I'd argue we're already there and people just haven't updated their workflows. For the general case, a colleague across arbitrary knowledge work, I'd say longer, because a lot of that work depends on context that isn't written down anywhere, and the agent has to learn to go get it.

The thing I'd caution against is the framing that there's some single moment where it flips. It's going to be gradual and uneven. You'll have agents that are better than you at one thing and embarrassingly bad at something adjacent, and the skill of the next few years is learning where that boundary is and moving it.

r001.rationale: It predicts that software engineering agents will be treated as colleagues within a couple of years.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what you mean by a competent colleague. If you mean someone you can give a fairly well-defined task to, who goes away for an hour and comes back with useful work, I think we're quite close. If you mean someone who understands all the context of your company, figures out what needs doing, and reliably makes good decisions over weeks, that's a much higher bar.

The distinction for me is how much supervision you need to provide. An agent can do something incredibly impressive, but if you have to check every step, you're still doing a lot of the work. It starts feeling like a colleague when you can delegate an outcome and trust it to ask for help when it's stuck.

So I expect that to happen gradually, in particular kinds of work first. I'm less confident about putting a date on the point where it works across everything.

r001.rationale: The response says agents are “quite close” for well-defined tasks, but gives no prediction in terms of a very small number of years.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what you mean by a competent colleague. If you mean someone you can give a well-defined task to, who works on it independently and comes back with something useful, we're already seeing pieces of that. If you mean someone who can handle ambiguity, notice when they're going in the wrong direction, and reliably deliver without much supervision, there's still a meaningful gap.

The hard part is consistency. An agent can do something incredibly impressive and then make a basic mistake a few steps later. For it to feel like a colleague, you need to be able to delegate without constantly checking its work. I expect we'll get there gradually, first in specific kinds of work, rather than on one particular day when agents suddenly become competent at everything.

r001.rationale: The response describes a remaining gap and gradual progress, but does not predict that agents will feel like competent colleagues within a very small number of years.
